messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Keller, a 56-year-old white American musician, came to treatment after more than a year of living in an ever-shrinking world. He was married and had spent most of his adult life playing evening sets in bars, hotel lounges, and private events, the kind of work that put him in crowded rooms where people drank, moved unpredictably, and wore strong scents. The assault had happened after a late gig at a private club. He had been packing up when a man connected to the venue, someone with a confident, controlling manner, cornered him in a back room. What Martin remembers most sharply are fragments: the smell of the man’s cologne when he was pinned close, a glimpse of blood after he was hurt, and the sudden violence of the man’s movements. Other parts fall away entirely. Even now he cannot give a continuous account of what happened from beginning to end; as he gets near the missing parts, his mind seems to shut a door.

In the weeks after, Martin found that the broken quality of the memory seemed to make ordinary moments dangerous. The clear shards—cologne, blood, abrupt motion—stood out with a terrible force because they were not embedded in a story he could place in the past. A man brushing by him in a hallway wearing a similar scent, a split knuckle on someone loading equipment, even an argument breaking out near a stage could hit him with the same sick jolt, as if his body had recognized the event before his mind had. Because so much of the assault remained blank, he was left scanning for these bits in the present, trying to catch danger from clues he did not fully understand.

That vigilance hardened quickly. Martin had come to feel safe only at home, in one room with the door locked, or in the small studio where he practiced alone. Outside those places he was on edge, especially if someone moved suddenly beside him. In clubs and rehearsal spaces, when a stagehand reached across him without warning or a patron lurched too close after drinking, he was instantly braced, heart racing, shoulders set. He had become irritable in ways that startled him; small interruptions could bring a sharp, angry snap, and he hated that side of himself. The violence in the room around him, even raised voices or rough joking, now seemed to prove that threat was everywhere.

As that sense of danger grew, Martin began organizing his life around avoiding what set it off. He stopped taking bookings that involved security staff, police presence, or venue managers in uniforms, because being around authority figures made his whole body tighten. He no longer joined the other musicians for drinks after a set and gradually stopped seeing friends he had socialized with before the assault; they belonged to the old music scene, and returning to them felt too exposed. He also worked hard never to let himself feel angry. Anger felt perilous to him, too close to the violence of that night, so he pressed it down until it came out sideways as irritability at home. These habits cost him work and left his wife increasingly aware of how confined and defensive he had become.

His way of dealing with the memory only deepened its fractured quality. Whenever an image began to form, Martin cut it off before it could fully arrive. He would distract himself, leave the room, pick up his guitar and run scales, anything to stop the recollection before it gathered momentum. The result was that the assault remained a set of isolated flashes—one unbearably clear moment followed by blankness—rather than something he could think through. Because he never stayed with it long enough to make sense of it, he remained unable to tell himself a coherent story, and each return of the fragments felt raw and immediate rather than known.

The same avoidance fed the power of his triggers. By steering clear of old friends, certain venues, and anyone in authority, he never had a chance to test whether every cue meant danger now. A trace of cologne in an elevator, blood on a bandmate’s finger during setup, or a scuffle outside a club door still landed with full force. And when those moments set off his alarm, the surge itself made the memory retreat again; he would feel the beginning of recognition, then clamp down, left only with the conviction that something terrible was about to happen. His wife finally urged him to seek help after he nearly walked out of a wedding performance when a guest in formalwear leaned in close, smelling of the same cologne, and another man made a sudden movement near the stage. Martin said what frightened him most was that his life had narrowed to a few safe places and a handful of rules, and even those no longer felt reliable. What he wanted, more than anything, was to be able to remember what happened without feeling that he was back there and to return to making music without bracing for danger in every room.
